stem.text: Holstein Friesian cattle are a breed of cattle used by dairy farmers in many countries of the world for the high milk yield of their cows.
Fig. 4.1 shows Holstein Friesian cattle.

stem.caption: Fig. 4.1
stem.alt: Photograph of several black-and-white Holstein Friesian cattle in a field, most lying down, one standing.

stem.text: Milk yield in Holstein Friesian cattle is affected by heat stress. Heat stress occurs when homeostatic mechanisms are not enough to keep the body temperature down to normal levels.
One of the factors that contributes to heat stress is air temperature.
Fig. 4.2 shows:

items: the mean daily air temperature in Central Europe
the mean monthly milk yield per cow of Holstein Friesian cattle in Central Europe.

stem.caption: Fig. 4.2
stem.alt: Bar chart by month (Jan-Dec) with two y-axes: mean daily air temperature in °C (left, 0-30) and mean monthly milk yield per cow in kg per cow (right, 550-850). Grey bars (temperature) rise from about 1°C in January to a peak of about 18°C in July-August, then fall to about 2°C in December. White bars (milk yield, each with a standard error bar) rise from about 720 kg in January to a peak of about 800 kg in April, dip slightly through summer, and fall to a low of about 685 kg around October-November before rising slightly in December.

stem.text: With reference to Fig. 4.2, describe the trends in air temperature and milk yield from April to August.

points.text: temperature increases and milk yield decreases ;
comparative data quote – April = 10 °C and 792–798 kg cow–1, August = 18 °C and 711–716 kg cow–1 ;

explanation.text: Read the two sets of bars over the same four months only (April to August), not the whole year: temperature rises over that stretch while milk yield falls, and a data quote comparing the April and August values for both variables supports the second mark.

reasoningChain: Compare temperature at April and August: it increases.
Compare milk yield at April and August: it decreases.
Quote approximate values for both variables at April and at August.

inferredMistakes.text: Describing the trend over the whole year instead of restricting the description to April to August as asked.
Misreading which axis or which key (grey vs white bars) corresponds to temperature and which to milk yield.

stem.text: Many dairy farmers in tropical regions use cattle breeds that are tolerant to heat stress (heat-tolerant cattle). These heat-tolerant cattle:

items: can tolerate higher air temperatures than Holstein Friesian cattle before heat stress occurs
have milder symptoms of heat stress than Holstein Friesian cattle for the same high air temperatures.

stem.text: Where heat stress does not occur, heat-tolerant cattle produce a lower milk yield than Holstein Friesian cattle under the same conditions.
Scientists compared DNA sequences of Holstein Friesian cattle and heat-tolerant cattle for a number of genes known to have an effect on body temperature.
Twenty genes were found that had alleles associated only with heat-tolerant cattle.
With reference to the information provided, including the data in Fig. 4.2:

items: state the type (pattern) of phenotypic variation shown by milk yield in cattle
identify factors that cause phenotypic variation in milk yield in cattle.

stem.text: In each case, give a reason for your choice.

labels: type (pattern) of phenotypic variation and reason for choice
factors that cause phenotypic variation and reason for each choice

points.text: continuous and (milk yield) does not fall into distinct classes / shows a range / intermediates / no distinct categories / AW ;
environment and (milk yield) affected by air temperature ;
genetic / polygenic and many / 20, genes have effect (on milk yield) or heat-tolerant cattle have lower milk yield than Holstein Friesian cattle ;

explanation.text: Each marking point is a type/factor paired with its reason, so each answer line really needs two things: the named pattern or factor, and the specific evidence for it. Milk yield is continuous because Fig. 4.2 shows it varying smoothly rather than in distinct categories.

Two different factors are asked for: an environmental factor, with air temperature from Fig. 4.2 as the evidence; and a genetic factor, with the twenty genes associated only with heat-tolerant cattle (or the yield difference between the two breeds under the same conditions) as the evidence.

reasoningChain: Classify the variation as continuous, because milk yield varies over a range rather than in distinct classes.
Identify air temperature (from Fig. 4.2) as an environmental factor affecting milk yield.
Identify the genes found in the DNA comparison as a genetic factor affecting milk yield, since many (20) genes are involved (polygenic).

inferredMistakes.text: Naming a factor (e.g. diet) that affects milk yield in general but that has no supporting evidence in the question's data.
Identifying the type or factor without giving the reason/evidence for the choice, when the question specifically asks for a reason in each case.

stem.text: The scientists found that one of the genes studied, PRLR, has a dominant allele known as SLICK. The SLICK allele was identified in Senepol cattle, a heat-tolerant breed, and is not found in Holstein Friesian cattle.
Cattle with the SLICK allele have short hair due to reduced hair growth.

Scientists have used selective breeding to introduce the SLICK allele into Holstein Friesian cattle. The milk yields of normal Holstein Friesian cattle and Holstein Friesian cattle with the SLICK allele are shown in Fig. 4.3, during:

items: March, when the mean daily air temperature is 5 °C.
September, when the mean daily air temperature is 14 °C.

stem.caption: Fig. 4.3
stem.alt: Bar chart of mean monthly milk yield per cow (kg per cow, 0-900) for March and September, each showing a white bar (Holstein Friesian cattle) and a grey bar (Holstein Friesian cattle with SLICK allele). March: about 780 kg (without SLICK) and about 795-800 kg (with SLICK). September: about 695-700 kg (without SLICK) and about 775-780 kg (with SLICK).

stem.text: With reference to Fig. 4.3, describe the effect of the SLICK allele on milk yield in Holstein Friesian cattle.

points.text: SLICK allele increases milk yield (in both months / at both temperatures) ;
in March / at 5 °C, there is a small difference (between milk yield) ;
in September / at 14 °C, there is a larger difference (between milk yields) ;
cattle with SLICK allele maintain milk yield (in both months / at both temperatures) ;
comparative data quote to support mp1–mp4 ;

markScheme.note: The MS table under 4(c) is reference data (the acceptable value ranges for the data-quote marking point), not a row-by-row marking grid; marks are awarded from the 5 points, any three.

explanation.text: Compare the paired bars at each month: in both March (5 °C) and September (14 °C) the SLICK bar is higher, so the allele increases milk yield at both temperatures. The size of the increase differs: small in March, when there is little or no heat stress, and larger in September, when the warmer temperature causes more heat stress in normal Holstein Friesian cattle, but SLICK cattle keep their yield up.

reasoningChain: Compare SLICK vs non-SLICK yield in March: higher with SLICK, small difference.
Compare SLICK vs non-SLICK yield in September: higher with SLICK, larger difference.
Link the larger September difference to SLICK cattle maintaining yield better as temperature/heat stress increases.
Support the comparison with approximate values read from the bars.

inferredMistakes.text: Describing only one month's bars (e.g. only September) instead of comparing both March and September as the figure shows.

stem.text: The SLICK allele differs from the recessive allele by a single nucleotide deletion. This results in a frameshift mutation and introduces a premature stop codon in the PRLR gene.
Scientists can use gene editing to replicate this mutation in Holstein Friesian cattle. This provides a way to introduce the SLICK allele into Holstein Friesian cattle without selective breeding.
Compare gene editing and selective breeding for introducing the SLICK allele into Holstein Friesian cattle.
Include similarities and differences in your answer.

points.text: (first) offspring have SLICK allele – true of both gene editing and selective breeding ;
can have, negative / unknown, effects – true of both gene editing and selective breeding ;
presence of SLICK allele (in offspring) can be confirmed by, genetic testing / phenotypic observation – true of both gene editing and selective breeding ;
done by humans / artificial methods – true of both gene editing and selective breeding ;
gene editing: only, PRLR / one, gene is affected and selective breeding: affects many genes ;
gene editing: all offspring have SLICK allele and selective breeding: some offspring have SLICK allele ;
gene editing: immediate / one generation and selective breeding: performed over (many) generations ;
gene editing: performed on, embryos / zygotes / cells and selective breeding: mating / artificial insemination ;
gene editing: technical requirements e.g. laboratory, training, molecular method and selective breeding: mating / performed on the farm e.g. physiological method ;
gene editing: maintains, heterozygosity / genetic variation / desirable characteristics and selective breeding: loss of, heterozygosity / genetic variation / desirable characteristics ;
gene editing: regulatory approval and selective breeding: no regulatory approval ;
gene editing: no outbreeding required and selective breeding: outbreeding required ;

markScheme.note: The MS prints points 1-4 as a two-column 'similarity' table (one statement true of both methods) and points 5-12 as paired left/right statements joined by 'and' for the two methods; the site's markScheme.table schema has no colspan, so this is kept as a plain points list (points 1-4 already spell out that each is shared by both methods) rather than forcing it into an asymmetric table.

explanation.text: 'Compare' means similarities AND differences are both expected. Four similarities: both methods can give offspring with the SLICK allele, both carry some risk of unintended effects, both results can be checked by testing or observation, and both are artificial (human-directed) rather than purely natural processes.

The differences follow from how each method actually works: gene editing changes one target gene directly in an embryo/cell in the lab, in one generation, affecting all edited offspring, needing technical/lab resources and regulatory approval; selective breeding works through mating over many generations, only some offspring inherit the allele, many genes besides PRLR are affected (so more variation/desirable traits can be lost), it needs no special lab approval but does need outbreeding to bring in the allele.

reasoningChain: Give at least one similarity (e.g. both are artificial methods done by humans).
Give several differences, each as a genuine two-sided comparison (gene editing does X, selective breeding does Y), not two separate unlinked lists.
Cover genes affected, proportion of offspring affected, timescale, where it is performed, technical/regulatory requirements, and effect on genetic variation.

inferredMistakes.text: Only describing differences and giving no similarity at all, even though the command word 'compare' and the question's own instruction both call for similarities as well.
Listing features of gene editing and features of selective breeding as two separate, unlinked lists rather than as paired comparative statements.

issues.note: MS 原文用一张两列对比表呈现（左列 gene editing，右列 selective breeding，部分行之间不分栏、是一句共同陈述），markScheme.table 目前没有 colspan，无法原样还原合并单元格。已改成纯 points 列表，points 1-4 的文字本身已经写明"两种方法都适用"，points 5-12 保留原文的左右对比句式（用 and 连接）。

bullets: Candidates who carefully noted the requirements of the question were able to describe the trends evident in the data. Many candidates did not take account of the limited time period over which the trends were to be identified and attempted to describe trends over the whole year. A significant proportion of candidates mis-read the axes or key.
Most candidates recognised the type of variation shown by milk yield and were able to give a reason for their choice.

Many candidates made effective use of the information provided and were able to identify, with reasons, relevant genetic and environmental factors that affect milk yield. A number suggested environmental factors for which there was no supporting data, such as diet, and some did not provide reasons for choosing the factors that they had identified.

The majority of candidates observed that the presence of the SLICK allele increases milk yield, with stronger responses describing the nuances at different temperatures when heat stress may or may not have a contributing effect.

Relatively few candidates attempted to identify similarities in the two methods, although this is always expected when the command word is ‘compare’ and, in this case, was specifically included in the question as an elaboration of the command word.

Most candidates indicated an awareness of differences between the two methods, but fewer structured their answers in a way that clearly identified these differences. Many simply listed features of the two methods separately without linking them into meaningful comparative statements.
